newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE - Canada pipeline race to produce winners and losers.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Canada pipeline race to produce winners and losers.

text.p: An unprecedented spate of proposals aimed at boosting Canadian gas exports to the United States is raising new questions over just how much capacity is too much and which pipelines will get built.
Planned and proposed pipeline projects aimed at moving more Canadian gas to the U.S. Midwest and northeast by the turn of the century are now valued at more than US$10 billion (C$13.8 billion).

Taken together, proposals on the drawing board represent an increase in Canadian export capacity of more than 8.5 billion cubic feet per day, approximately three-quarters of the gas produced each day in the province of Alberta's gas basin.

"There's no way in the world that all the projects that have been announced lately will go in the time frame that the project developers are talking about," said Roland George, vice-president of the Canadian Energy Research Institute.
"There would be just too much pipe capacity coming on too quickly, and if you put all that capacity in, you start to ask whether the basin can support that."
TRANSCANADA IS DOMINANT PLAYER

Over the past month, billions of dollars worth of new pipelines and expansions have been announced by such firms as Coastal Corp, Northern States Power Co, Columbia Gas System Inc, Westcoast Energy Inc and CMS Energy Corp.
New projects include the Viking Voyageur Gas Transmission line to the U.S. Midwest from Emerson, Manitoba and the Great Lakes Gas Transmission expansion and Millenium Pipeline to the Northeast.

These, which would all be in service by the year 2000, are on top of the Northern Border Partners LP 700 million cubic feet per day (MMCFD) expansion and extension to Chicago slated to be in service by the end of 1998.

The New England region is also set for over 480 MMCFD of gas that would flow from the proposed Sable Island gas project offshore Nova Scotia as well as 178 MMCFD from the planned Portland Natural Gas Transmission system.

The dominant player in the race -- and the key firm in nearly all the proposals -- is TransCanada PipeLines Ltd, which operates Canada's seven billion cubic feet a day mainline. It would transport gas to all the just-announced pipelines and has a stake in most of them.

TransCanada, which will add 289 MMCFD of capacity this year, could boost its total by 1.4 billion cubic feet per day by the turn of the century under its so-called Nexus staged expansion programme which will ship the new gas to Emerson, Manitoba.
CANADIAN MARKET SHARE IN U.S. SEEN STATIC
CERI forecasts show Canada's total gas output is expected to rise to about seven trillion cubic feet annually by the year 2010, including export volumes of 3.7 TCF.
That's an increase from total output of 5.41 TCF in 1996, with 2.8 TCF being shipped to the United States for about 13 percent of U.S. demand.
While gas demand in the U.S. is expected to grow by one to two percent a year over the next decade, Canada's market share is projected to stay in the 12-14 percent range, George said.
Ron Barrone, a New York-based pipeline analyst with PaineWebber, said the U.S. has the ability to absorb all the gas Canada can send, but not without dire consequences on U.S. prices.

Today's hot pipeline activity contrasts sharply to just two years ago, when Canadian gas producers, hammered by far lower prices than those in the U.S., were criticising pipeline companies for not providing enough export space to meet growing production.
Starting in late 1994, the spread between Canadian natural gas prices and NYMEX Henry Hub prices, the U.S. benchmark, began to widen.
By the summer of 1996, when Henry Hub gas was fetching about US$2.70 per million British thermal units, prices at the AECO-C Hub, Canada's main pricing point, were around US$0.90 per mmBtu.

The "natural" basis differential, or transport rate without taking into account factors like capacity constraints or regional short-term price fluctuations, has been estimated at about US$0.50 per mmBtu, George said.
ALLIANCE WAS THE TRIGGER

Canadian producers and analysts have long said that, without more takeaway capacity from Alberta, Canada's biggest producing province, gas was being trapped within its borders and competition to sell it was driving prices down.
Industry officials say the trigger for today's explosion of competing proposals was the development of the producer-backed Alliance Pipeline project.

Alliance, a consortium of 18 companies including Alberta Energy Co Ltd, Gulf Canada Resources Ltd, Chevron Corp Canada Resources and IPL Energy Inc, aims to ship 1.3 billion cubic feet of gas a day to Chicago from northeast British Columbia, a 3,000 km (1,864 mile) route.
The project, with an estimated cost of C$3.6 billion ($2.6 billion), would be in service by late 1999. It is currently before regulators in Canada and the United States.

"Alliance was proposed first while the other guys in the long-line pipeline business were kind of sitting on their hands. We got it going as a group of producers," said Gwyn Morgan, chief executive of Alberta Energy.
"A year or two later, when it's well under way, they now have all kinds of ideas."
TransCanada spokesman David Annesley disagreed, saying his company's plans were more of a reaction to export opportunities than producer-backed pipelines.
"I think it's a question of, when did the market develop," he said.
Despite strong support for Alliance, analysts wonder whether its partners may loosen their resolve to build the line now that TransCanada and its allies have proposed the new projects.

"The question is, are the producers up in Canada rattling their swords for better rates and to get some pipe capacity built, or are they serious that they don't want to be dependent upon other shippers?" Barrone said.
One thing is for sure, George said: the days of pipeline companies having sole power to control capacity additions are over.

"Transportation is increasingly becoming a competitive commodity service that can be provided, not just by one entity, but several entities. So that anybody not willing to play the competitive game encounters some serious problems," he said.
